See [the reusable kernel contract](kernel.md) for application ownership and the
non-research execution proof, and [installation boundaries](installations.md) for
independent records and runtime lifecycles. These remain inside this repository.

The local [improvement application](improvements.md) uses that same kernel contract
in an explicitly new experiment record. Captured public research informs code
proposals; it does not become writable research authority. Untrusted candidate
code runs only in restricted disposable containers, while the host scores its
outputs. An operator review receipt cannot apply code or grant release authority.

The [autonomous context lane](autonomous-context.md) is a separate WAKE application
policy on the existing per-node native authority. An installed capability permits
one selector-field change, gated by recomputed fixed-task and current-native-state
measurements. Proposal generation, adoption and rollback require no per-change
human review. Metadata events preserve research versions and history; candidate
data cannot replace the evaluator, widen permissions, modify code or create a
competing research store. Native replay owns the policy after restart.

> **Current specification.** This document explains why the present system is shaped this way: its trust boundary, durable record, governance model and known limits. Current local procedures belong in `standalone.md`; public mirror publishing belongs in `cloud.md`. Maintainer navigation, environment checks and reproducible validation guidance belong in `development.md`.

**WAKE✳︎** is infrastructure for continuity of accountable work, not continuity of a model instance. Its stable sequence is **Record → Context → Proposal → Governance → Transition → Receipt**. id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2005.12543v3
published: 2020-05-26T06:56:58Z
summary: We propose a definition of persistent Stiefel-Whitney classes of vector bundle filtrations. It relies on seeing vector bundles as subsets of some Euclidean spaces. The usual Čech filtration of such a subset can be endowed with a vector bundle structure, that we call a Čech bundle filtration. We show that this construction is stable and consistent. When the dataset is a finite sample of a line bundle, we implement an effective algorithm to compute its persistent Stiefel-Whitney classes. In order to use simplicial approximation techniques in practice, we develop a notion of weak simplicial approximation. As a theoretical example, we give an in-depth study of the normal bundle of the circle, which reduces to understanding the persistent cohomology of the torus knot (1,2). We illustrate our method on several datasets inspired by image analysis.

title: Stabilizing the unstable output of persistent homology computations
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/1512.01700v5
published: 2015-12-05T20:42:33Z
summary: We propose a general technique for extracting a larger set of stable information from persistent homology computations than is currently done. The persistent homology algorithm is usually viewed as a procedure which starts with a filtered complex and ends with a persistence diagram. This procedure is stable (at least to certain types of perturbations of the input). This justifies the use of the diagram as a signature of the input, and the use of features derived from it in statistics and machine learning. However, these computations also produce other information of great interest to practitioners that is unfortunately unstable. For example, each point in the diagram corresponds to a simplex whose addition in the filtration results in the birth of the corresponding persistent homology class, but this correspondence is unstable. As AI-mediated decisions spread across organizations, accountability is often addressed through legal liability, ethics guidelines, or ad hoc managerial responses. This paper argues that such approaches fail to capture a deeper structural problem: accountability collapses when decision authority, exception response, and responsibility are not coherently aligned. We conceptualize accountability as a protocol rather than a role or rule, and examine how responsibility becomes displaced onto individuals or functions when decision boundaries are undefined. The paper demonstrates why existing organizational roles cannot absorb this burden and why accountability must be designed as part of decision infrastructure. Perspectives of and recommendations by caregivers and hospice staff.\", \"abstract\": \"

Background and objectives

Tools powered by artificial intelligence (AI) are reshaping many aspects of dementia care, and end-of-life caregiving for persons with dementia may not be exempt from such paradigm shifts. In this study, we explored families' and staff's acceptance of AI in hospice dementia care and generated actionable recommendations for AI designers in supporting end-of-life care for persons with dementia.

Design and methods

In this qualitative descriptive study, we conducted individual and focus group interviews with family caregivers (N = 30) of hospice patients with dementia and hospice staff (N = 9). We utilized the Technology Acceptance Model as our theoretical framework and conducted directed content analysis.

Results

Participants described AI tools as potentially helpful for obtaining information, monitoring patients, managing medications and appointments, providing companionship, and conducting logistical tasks. Familiarity with technology, along with user-friendly interfaces and guidance, emerged as subcategories of perceived ease of use. The uniqueness of hospice, encompassing its humanistic nature and emphasis on families as part of the care unit, also emerged as a key factor impacting attitudes towards AI use. Although many anticipated that AI would bring inevitable changes in the future, they showed nuanced trust and perspectives on how it would impact the essence of care. Based on our participants' narratives, recommendations emerged across three domains: population-related, AI feature-related, and deployment-related.

Discussion and implications
